summary:
MAXQMOON — Lunar Observation & Landing-Site Planner

MAXQMOON is a NASA Space Apps project that lets you explore lunar observation conditions and identify potential landing sites using real scientific data—not mock data.
Main features

    2D sky view: See where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the terrain horizon.

    3D surface view: Explore measured lunar terrain, use compass controls, and switch on a night-vision mode that brings out the relief.

    3D Moon/system view: Pick locations on the globe and see the active observation point.

    Visibility planning: Calculate sunlight and Earth-visibility windows for a chosen location and date range.

    A/B comparison: Compare two locations selected from the catalog, map, or globe.

    Candidate discovery: Find and rank locations by sunlight, Earth visibility, terrain slope, and timing—without having to choose A/B points first.

    English/Turkish interface: Switch languages across charts, controls, planning screens, and scientific notes.
details:
MAXQMOON is an interactive tool built to help anyone exploring potential lunar landing and observation sites answer three practical questions: When will sunlight reach this spot, when will Earth be visible from here, and how do the surrounding craters and mountains affect both? Users can either pick a location from a preset catalog or click anywhere on an interactive 3D lunar map to check its elevation and slope, and even compare two different sites side by side. On top of that, instead of guessing, users can enter their own requirements—like minimum sunlight hours, Earth visibility, or maximum slope—to automatically discover the best matching spots on the Moon.

Behind the scenes, the app brings together real laser elevation data from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) and scientific planetary data packages (NAIF SPICE and JPL). It calculates the exact positions of the Sun and Earth from the perspective of someone standing on the Moon, then checks if the surrounding terrain blocks the view. The results are displayed across three connected screens: a 2D sky chart showing the Sun and Earth against the local horizon, a 3D ground-level view that makes you feel like you are standing right on the lunar surface, and a 3D lunar globe for geographic context. A shared timeline at the bottom lets you scrub through different dates and times to watch how lighting and visibility change in real time.

Even when orbital math says the Sun or Earth should be visible, the Moon's rugged terrain can easily get in the way. By making these shadow and blockage effects easy to see, MAXQMOON helps users explore early ideas around solar power, direct-to-Earth communication, and safe landing zones. Our goal is to make complex lunar data accessible and fun to explore for students, researchers, and space enthusiasts. Of course, this isn't a flight-certified system for a real space mission, but rather an educational and early-stage planning tool.

We built the entire project on a regular Linux computer without needing any special hardware. For the user interface, we used TypeScript, React, and Three.js for the 3D visuals, while the backend scientific calculations run on Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SpiceyPy, and Rasterio. To make sure everything works smoothly, we wrote and passed 174 frontend tests and 365 backend tests. Right now, the web interface is hosted on Vercel and connects to our local calculation engine via a Cloudflare Tunnel.

What makes MAXQMOON unique is how it connects raw numbers directly to a human perspective. Instead of just showing flat maps or boring data tables, it lets you step right onto the Moon, look around at the horizon, and see how things change over time. Plus, its criteria-based search flips the usual process around by letting you describe what you need first and finding the right locations for you.

Throughout development, we focused heavily on scientific honesty and ease of use. We made sure all data sources and calculation rules are completely transparent, and we never generated fake terrain for areas where NASA data is missing. We also added both English and Turkish language support so more people can use it comfortably. Finally, we made sure to be clear about the tool's limits: seeing the Sun doesn't guarantee a working power grid, and seeing Earth doesn't automatically mean a strong radio link. Keeping these boundaries clear makes the project genuinely useful without overpromising.
